newsitem.title: THAILAND: Baht hit by finance portfolio rumour, economy woes.
newsitem.headline: Baht hit by finance portfolio rumour, economy woes.

text.p: Thailand intervened on Wednesday to defend the baht against fresh market attacks, and its central bank warned of taking more actions to counter market pressure on the currency.
The Bank of Thailand said it teamed up with the Monetary Authority of Singapore to intervene in the Singapore market to stabilise the baht.
Analysts said the intervention, the first joint action confirmed by the two central banks, came after the baht fell to 26.250-26.300 to the dollar.
The Thai currency recovered to 26.030-26.080 after the central bank action, but it was quoted sharply weaker at 26.550-26.750 during off-hour trading late on Wednesday.
"I don't know if the baht would see a calmer market tomorrow. It still looks weak and fragile after intervention," a dealer at a foreign bank said.
But another currency trader at Thai Military Bank Plc said she expected speculators to lie low on Thursday after the central bank showed its determination to back the currency.

The Bank of Thailand said: "This concerted operation is aimed at stemming excessive speculative activities which may lead to disorderly conditions in the Thai and regional financial markets. Other appropriate measures will be taken as necessary."

The baht's woes were partly triggered by suggestions last weekend by members in Prime Minister Chavalit Yongchaiyudh's coalition for Finance Minister Amnuay Viravan to resign and take responsibility for Thailand's mounting economic problems.
Amnuay told Reuters in Tokyo, after attending a meeting of the Asian Development Bank in the Japanese city of Fukuoka, that he was confident of his future as finance minister.
He said Thailand was committed to maintaining baht stability and its central bank would succeed in turning back any further market attacks on the currency.
Chavalit on Tuesday voiced his full backing for Amnuay. The prime minister also ruled out any plan to devalue the baht.
The Thai economy is in its worst shape in 10 years with gross domestic product projected to expand about five to six percent, against 6.7 percent in 1996 and 8.6 percent in 1995.

The attacks on the baht sent more shock waves through the ailing stock market, where the Composite Index plunged 4.82 percent to a near eight-year low of 571.30 points on Wednesday. The index has lost 13.6 percent this month.
Finance ministry officials and some private bankers said the damage from a baht devaluation would outweigh benefits for the Thai economy.

They said a devaluation would not substantially help Thai exports as more than 75 percent were industrial products with high import contents. The officials said a devalued baht would instead sharply raise the financing costs of Thailand's estimated $90 billion foreign debt.
"Efforts to dampen speculation on Amnuay's future were not helped by his absence," a dealer at Hongkong and Shanghai Bank said. Amnuay is not due back in Bangkok until Saturday.

Assistant central bank governor Siri Ganjarerndee attributed the attack on the baht to negative market perception of the Thai economy and to rumours of possible economic policy and finance portfolio changes.
He told reporters the rumours prompted a market flight to the dollar from baht, a move sharply tightening short-term domestic liquidity.
